title: It’s Tokens All The Way Down: How RLMs are Different — Kevin Madura, AlixPartners
talk_summary: Kevin Madura explains recursive language models (RLMs): the model works inside a symbolic REPL, stores large context as variables, writes code to inspect it, and recursively delegates subproblems to itself or other LMs. He argues this reduces context rot and token bloat, with examples on dataframes, invoices, traces, and large codebases.

takeaways.what_they_do: RLM stores large inputs as variables in a Python REPL; the model writes code to inspect, filter, and compute over them, pulling only distilled results into its context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it treats the context as an object that it can interact with symbolically in its environment
takeaways.numbers: 2.6% to 45.4% accuracy on long chain of thought benchmark

takeaways.what_they_do: The main model calls sub-LMs with enforced input/output schemas, so cheap models get precise typed handoffs instead of loose strings.
takeaways.evidence_quote: predict RLM uses DSPI to determine the schemas between the main LM and the subLM calls

takeaways.what_they_do: The RLM has a max-iteration variable and decides when to call submit with the final typed output instead of running indefinitely.
Halo uses an RLM over long agent traces to recommend improvements to the harness itself rather than only tuning one workflow.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's actually iterating on the harness. So it's like a meta abstraction almost or meta optimization of the harness itself

takeaways.what_they_do: An RLM can scan an arbitrarily large codebase by writing code and delegating chunks, then aggregate a security report without stuffing all code into context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: run through whatever it is 500,000 lines of code to generate some type of security report
